extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (Kantian teleology and aesthetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for using the concept of natural purposiveness (teleology) in judgment: when it may be applied, whether it can be used dogmatically, and how it relates to mechanical explanation. Focused on Kant's distinction between reflective and determinant judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reflective and determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A concept is used dogmatically (determinant judgement) when it is subsumed under another concept of the Object as constitutive; it is used critically (reflective judgement) when considered only with reference to our cognitive faculties without deciding about the Object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the concept of a natural purpose dogmatically for determinant judgements unless its objective reality is first assured; use it critically (as a reflective principle) to guide inquiry into natural products when objective proof is not available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of natural purpose is regulative, not constitutive
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of a thing as a natural purpose cannot be proven by Reason to have objective reality and therefore is not constitutive for determinant judgements, but is a regulative principle for reflective judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the concept of purposiveness as a maxim guiding investigation and reflection (it is indispensable for judging organised natural products) but recognize it cannot establish objective claims about the nature of things independent of our cognitive standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the maxim of design as a necessary heuristic for empirical study
rubrics_metrics.description: We are indispensably obliged to ascribe the concept of design to nature (at least for organised products) if we wish to investigate them by continuous observation; this maxim is an absolutely necessary principle for the empirical use of Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the idea of design as a guiding thread when studying organised beings to discover laws that would otherwise remain hidden, while remembering this is a methodological maxim and not proof of an actual designing cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement cannot dogmatically prove an intelligent original Being
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology does not prove objectively that there is an intelligent original Being; it only shows that, for the constitution of our cognitive faculties, we cannot think certain natural possibilities except by representing a designedly-working supreme cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit teleological conclusions to subjective justification for using the notion of a designing cause in human judgement; avoid asserting objective theological claims (e.g., 'There is a God') on teleological grounds alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular explanations deriving purposiveness from life or mechanism a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations that attempt to derive the purposiveness of nature in organised beings from living matter or from purely mechanical principles encounter circularity or are not possible a priori; such hypotheses cannot secure the objective reality of purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume hylozoism or purely mechanical accounts provide a priori justification for purposiveness; recognize when an explanation is circular (deriving life from matter while only knowing life in organised beings) and treat such accounts as inadequate for dogmatic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human discursive understanding necessitates representing organised beings as if designed
rubrics_metrics.description: Because our understanding is discursive (proceeds from universal concepts to particulars) and the particular is contingent relative to the universal, we must represent certain natural products (organised beings) as if produced according to purposes to make their possibility intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging organised natural products, account for the contingency introduced by our discursive cognition and accept that treating them 'as if' designed is a consequence of our cognitive constitution, not proof of design in the things themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate an intellectus archetypus as a regulative Idea if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: To think the necessary accordance of natural laws with our judgement we may posit an intuitive understanding (intellectus archetypus) as an Idea; this does not prove such an understanding exists but serves as a regulative concept to make purposiveness thinkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the notion of a higher/intuitive understanding only as a heuristic regulative Idea to account for unity and purposiveness; do not treat it as a constitutive, empirically established entity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve mechanical explanation while employing teleology
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of infinite importance not to neglect the mechanism of nature in explanations; mechanical derivation of purposive products is compatible with teleological judgement, but teleology does not remove the necessity of mechanical inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scientific practice, pursue mechanical explanations of natural products and do not abandon them when using teleological principles; avoid tautological explanations that merely reassert design without providing mechanistic understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize subjective validity of possibility vs actuality distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between possibility and actuality has merely subjective validity for human understanding because our knowledge requires both concepts (understanding) and sensible intuition; Reason's demand for an unconditioned ground (necessary being) is a problematical Idea unattainable constitutionally by understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about inferring actuality from mere possibility; acknowledge that Reason's unconditioned Ideas guide thought but do not confer objective knowledge of such grounds.
